stops.name: Yapeyú, mission town on the Uruguay
stops.campa: In the reduction of Nuestra Señora de los Tres Reyes de Yapeyú, where the mission bells still ring over the great river, José Francisco is born to Don Juan de San Martín, lieutenant governor, and Doña Gregoria Matorras. Guaraní nurses carry the child under the orange trees; the river runs north to south like a prophecy. The land itself, tradition says, marks him: a son of the Missions, born on the frontier of two worlds, destined to unmake an empire.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the child in the viceregal city
stops.campa: Don Juan is posted to the capital and the family takes a house near the Plaza Mayor. The boy learns his first letters within sound of the fort's cannon and the cathedral bells of Buenos Aires, the city to which, though he does not know it, he will return as a soldier, and to which his heart will return last of all. Ox-carts, candle-sellers, the mud of the unpaved streets: the small patria fixes itself in him.

stops.name: Río de la Plata, embarkation on the Santa Balbina
stops.campa: The family boards the frigate Santa Balbina for Spain. Five-year-old José watches the low shore of the Plata sink behind the ship, the first of the ocean partings that will measure his life. The tradition counts them: he leaves America a child of the King and will return a knight of a secret oath. The long Atlantic passage begins his apprenticeship to distance, patience, and the sea.

stops.name: Cádiz, first landfall in Spain
stops.campa: The white city on its spit of Atlantic rock receives the boy from the Missions. Cádiz, port of the Indies fleets, city of merchants and liberal talk, is his first Spain, and the canon marks the symmetry: here he lands as a child, and from here, twenty-seven years later, he will sail back with the oath of American liberty under his tongue. The family passes on toward Madrid, seeking a posting and schooling for the sons.

stops.name: Málaga, the schoolboy on Calle Pozos Dulces
stops.campa: The family settles in Málaga, in a house on Calle Pozos Dulces. José studies grammar, arithmetic and drawing at the Escuela de Temporalidades; he shows the traits the tradition will canonize: few words, exact habits, a gravity beyond his years. The Mediterranean light, the garrison drums, the talk of wars against Moor and Frenchman: the boy's road bends already toward the barracks.

stops.name: Málaga, cadet of the Regiment of Murcia
stops.campa: At eleven years old José signs as cadet in the Regiment of Murcia, 'el Leal'. The same month the Bastille falls in Paris; the boy puts on the white coat of the Bourbon infantry as the old world begins to burn. Twenty-two years in the armies of the King begin here: drill, musket, the ordinances learned by heart, the iron schooling he will one day turn against the crown that gave it.

stops.name: Oran, baptism of fire against the Moors
stops.campa: In the besieged African plaza of Oran, thirteen-year-old San Martín hears shot fired in anger for the first time. For more than thirty days the batteries thunder against the Moorish lines; the cadet stands his watch on the walls among veterans twice his size. The tradition keeps this as his baptism of fire: the boy who does not flinch, formed under bombardment on the last ember of Spanish Africa.

stops.name: Roussillon, the war against the French Convention
stops.campa: In the Pyrenean campaigns against revolutionary France, the adolescent officer fights at the sieges and mountain combats of the Roussillon. He is promoted second lieutenant for valor under fire; he learns mountain war: columns threaded through passes, supply trains, the cold that kills more surely than lead. The canon reads it as rehearsal: in these Pyrenees the crosser of the Andes serves his apprenticeship, in the army of the King he will one day defeat.

stops.name: At sea off Cape Palos, the Santa Dorotea and HMS Lion
stops.campa: Serving as a marine aboard the frigate Santa Dorotea, San Martín fights the ship of the line HMS Lion off the Levantine coast. Outgunned, dismasted, her decks running, the frigate strikes only when resistance is beyond reason. The young officer is briefly a prisoner of the English, the nation whose ships will one day carry him to London, to Buenos Aires, and into exile. The sea marks its man.

stops.name: Cádiz, the murder of General Solano
stops.campa: Napoleon's armies hold Madrid; Spain rises. In Cádiz the mob storms the palace of the captain-general, the Marquis of Solano, San Martín's own chief and protector, and drags him to his death for hesitating to fire on the French fleet. The aide-de-camp sees the crowd do murder in the name of patriotism. The canon dates from this day his lifelong horror of anarchy and of the mob: order, discipline, the law, or the abyss.

stops.name: Arjonilla, the lance combat
stops.campa: Leading a handful of horsemen against a French cavalry patrol near Arjonilla, San Martín is unhorsed in the melee; a French dragoon's sabre is at his throat when the soldier Juan de Dios throws himself between and takes the blow. The skirmish is won, the young officer's name is mentioned in the dispatches of the Andalusian army; and the pattern is set that San Lorenzo will repeat: the fallen commander, the soldier who dies so that the destiny may live.

stops.name: Bailén, the first defeat of Napoleon's eagles
stops.campa: In the olive groves and burning July dust of Bailén, the Spanish army of Castaños forces the surrender of General Dupont's corps, the first capitulation of a Napoleonic army in open field anywhere in Europe. San Martín, fighting with distinction under the Count of Coupigny, is promoted lieutenant colonel and receives the gold medal of Bailén. He has seen the invincible beaten; the lesson travels with him across the ocean: empires fall to disciplined resolve.
